notes.text: 背 (bèi) = the upper back. Chinese splits the back in two: 腰 (yāo) is the lower back/waist, and 腰疼 is a different complaint entirely.

notes.text: The colloquial belly — what hurts, what gets full (肚子饱了). 胃 (wèi) is the stomach organ specifically, as in 胃疼 or 胃不好.
The upper back. Note the reading: 背 is bèi as a noun but bēi as the verb "to carry on one's back."
大腿 = thigh, 小腿 = calf — Chinese builds them off the same root.
Goes after the body part, not before: 头疼, 背疼, 肚子疼. 痛 (tòng) means the same thing and dominates in writing and in Taiwan.
头 (head) + 发 (hair) — only hair on the head. 毛 (máo) covers body and animal hair. Second syllable is neutral tone here, though 发 is fā elsewhere.
Neutral tone on the second syllable — this is the pair that trips everyone up against 眼镜 (glasses).
眼镜 (jìng, 4th tone) = glasses vs 眼睛 (jing, neutral) = eyes. Near-identical to the ear at speed; the tone is the whole difference. 戴眼镜 = to wear glasses.

examples.english: He has a high nose bridge.

Distinct from 腿 (leg) — Chinese does not blur them.

examples.english: It's ten miles from here to the airport.

notes.text: 离……很近 = close to…

examples.pinyin: Wǒ jiā lí gōngyuán hěn jìn.
examples.english: My home is very close to the park.

notes.text: 在……旁边 = next to. 在我旁边 = next to me.

examples.english: The pharmacy is next to the bank.

notes.text: 北京 = northern capital, 南京 = southern capital.

examples.english: The train station is on the north side.

notes.text: 在桌子上面 = on top of the table. In practice 上 alone often suffices: 桌子上.

examples.english: The phone is on the table.

notes.text: 外边 is the same word. 在外面吃 = to eat out.
右边 (yòubian) = the right side. Chinese always names them in the order 左右, which is also the word for "approximately."

examples.english: The subway station is on the right.

notes.text: This, not 方, is the actual word for "side." Interchangeable with 面 as a locative suffix: 左边/左面, 里边/里面.

examples.english: Let's go for a walk by the sea.

notes.text: Chinese recites the compass as 东南西北, and the combinations reverse English: 东北 = northeast, 西南 = southwest.

examples.english: The subway station is on the south side of the park.

notes.text: 那儿 (nàr) in the north. 哪里 (nǎlǐ, where) differs only in tone — listen for nǎ vs nà.
Also a verb, "to arrive" — 我到了 = I'm here. 到了 = arrived.
迷 (to be confused) + 路 (road).
直 (straight) + 走. 一直走 = keep going straight.

examples.english: Go straight and you'll be there.

notes.text: Literally "to sit" — 坐地铁, 坐火车, 坐飞机. 骑 for bikes, 开 for driving yourself.

examples.english: I take the subway to the office.

notes.text: 打 again. 打的 (dǎdī) is the older slang; ride apps mostly killed street hailing anyway.

examples.english: Let's take a taxi to the airport.

notes.text: 换 (to change) + 乘 (to ride). On signage everywhere in subways.

examples.english: I transfer at this subway station.

notes.text: 拐 (guǎi) = to turn a corner. 左转 (zuǒ zhuǎn) is the more formal/driving-instruction version.

examples.english: Turn left when you reach the intersection.

notes.text: Mirror of the above.

examples.english: Turn right when you get to the park.

notes.text: 走路去 = to go on foot.
往前走 = keep going forward, 往左拐 = turn left. 向 (xiàng) is the slightly more formal alternative.
A location — 在楼上.
东西 (dōngxi, east-west) as a compound means "thing/stuff" — a useful accident to remember.

examples.pinyin: Gōngyuán zài xuéxiào de xī biān.
examples.english: The park is on the west side of the school.

notes.text: 哪里 / 哪儿 — 儿 forms are northern/Beijing-flavored, 里 forms more universal. Careful with 那里 (nàlǐ, there): 哪 (nǎ) asks, 那 (nà) points.

examples.pinyin: Qiánmiàn shì yí ge cháng lùkǒu.
examples.english: Up ahead is a long block.

examples.hanzi: 前面有一个急转，你开车要慢一点儿。

examples.english: There's a sharp turn ahead, so drive a bit slower.

notes.text: Also very common with time: 大约三点 (dàyuē sān diǎn, around 3 o'clock), 大约一个小时 (about an hour).

examples.hanzi: 从这里到机场大约一个小时。
examples.pinyin: Cóng zhèlǐ dào jīchǎng dàyuē yí ge xiǎoshí.
examples.english: It's about an hour from here to the airport.

notes.text: 左右 goes after the number (十个左右 = 10-ish), and feels a bit more casual/spoken.

examples.hanzi: 我们等了一个小时左右。
examples.pinyin: Wǒmen děng le yí ge xiǎoshí zuǒyòu.
examples.english: We waited for about an hour.

notes.text: Very versatile — can praise someone's skill ("you're amazing") or describe something intense/severe depending on context and tone.
Basic temperature adjective, opposite of 热 (hot).
Basic temperature adjective, opposite of 冷 (cold).
Used to soften a comparison, e.g. 比较好 (relatively good/pretty good).
Basic flavor adjective.
生 (to produce) + 气 (air/temper). Two patterns: 对我生气 or the split form 生我的气 — the possessive slots inside the verb.
The opposite of 脏 (zāng). 打扫干净 = to clean something until it is clean — 干净 works as a result complement.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ yǒu yí ge hēisè de bāo.
Tā de chē shì lánsè de.

notes.text: Placed before a color for a bright, eye-catching, almost neon effect — 亮黄色 (neon yellow), 亮粉色 (neon pink). 亮 on its own also just means "bright/shiny" (e.g. for lights).

examples.pinyin: wǒ de gǒu shì zōngsè de.

notes.text: Placed before a color to mean "dark/deep" — 深蓝色, 深红色. Also means "deep" generally (深水) and "profound."

examples.english: The ocean here is very deep.

notes.text: 深 + 蓝色 — a very common way to say "navy/dark blue," for clothes, cars, ink, etc.

examples.hanzi: 我想买一条深蓝色的裤子。
examples.pinyin: wǒ xiǎng mǎi yì tiáo shēn lánsè de kùzi.
examples.english: I want to buy a pair of navy pants.

examples.pinyin: tā de chē shì shēn lǜsè de.

examples.hanzi: 她买了一件深红色的衣服。
examples.pinyin: tā mǎi le yí jiàn shēn hóngsè de yīfu.
examples.english: She bought a dark red top.

notes.text: Refers to the color gold, but is also the go-to word for describing blonde hair. Not used for the metal gold itself (that's 黄金, huángjīn).

examples.pinyin: tā de tóufa shì jīnsè de.
wǒ de diànnǎo shì huīsè de.
wǒ de zìxíngchē shì lǜsè de.

notes.text: Placed before a color to mean "light/pale" — 浅蓝色 (light blue), 浅绿色 (light green). The more universal of the two "light" modifiers.
Also means "light/pale," but leans toward a delicate, washed-out, or subtle shade — 淡黄色 (pale yellow), 淡紫色 (pale lavender). Often preferred for soft, muted tones; 浅 is more neutral/general-purpose.

examples.english: This soup is a bit bland.

examples.pinyin: wǒ yǒu yì shuāng qiǎn lánsè de xié.
examples.english: I have a pair of light blue shoes.

examples.hanzi: 妹妹想买浅紫色的雨伞。
examples.pinyin: mèimei xiǎng mǎi qiǎn zǐsè de yǔsǎn.
examples.english: My little sister wants to buy a lavender umbrella.

examples.hanzi: 她的手机是亮粉色的，很可爱。
examples.pinyin: tā de shǒujī shì liàng fěnsè de, hěn kě'ài.
examples.english: Her phone is neon pink — so cute.

examples.hanzi: 那辆亮黄色的车太贵了。
examples.pinyin: nà liàng liàng huángsè de chē tài guì le.
examples.english: That neon yellow car is too expensive.

notes.text: 色 is kept here because 橙 on its own means the orange fruit — the bare syllable would be ambiguous in a way 红/蓝/绿 are not.

examples.pinyin: wǒ de qiánbāo shì chéngsè de.

notes.text: 淡 + 黄色 — a soft, muted yellow. 淡 fits here better than 浅 for this gentle, washed-out shade.

examples.hanzi: 这条淡黄色的裤子很好看。
examples.pinyin: zhè tiáo dàn huángsè de kùzi hěn hǎokàn.
examples.english: These pale yellow pants look great.

notes.text: 粉色 is the common everyday term; 粉红色 (fěnhóngsè, literally "powder-red") means the same thing and is a bit more descriptive/formal, but both are used interchangeably in speech.

examples.pinyin: wǒ nǚ'ér de chuáng shì fěnsè de.

examples.hanzi: 那件紫色的衣服很漂亮。
examples.pinyin: nà jiàn zǐsè de yīfu hěn piàoliang.
examples.english: That purple top is really pretty.

notes.text: The all-purpose word for red — also carries cultural weight (luck, celebration) in Chinese contexts.

examples.pinyin: wǒ xiǎng mǎi yí ge hóngsè de bāo.
examples.english: I want to buy a red bag.

notes.text: Refers to the color silver (metallic or otherwise); for silver/gray hair specifically, 银发 (yínfà) is the more literary/set term.

examples.pinyin: wǒ bàba de chē shì yínsè de.
Wǒ de māo shì báisè de.

notes.text: Fantasy — magic, other worlds. 科幻 (kēhuàn) = sci-fi, 玄幻 (xuánhuàn) = Chinese-style fantasy with cultivation and immortals, 武侠 (wǔxiá) = martial-arts fiction.

examples.pinyin: Zhè bù qíhuàn diànyǐng hěn hǎokàn.
examples.english: This fantasy movie is really good.

notes.text: 最 is the superlative marker and goes before any adjective — 最大 (biggest), 最贵 (most expensive), 最喜欢 (favorite). 最好 also means "had better": 你最好早点去.

examples.pinyin: Tā shì wǒ zuì hǎo de péngyou.

notes.text: Also a friendly prefix for people younger than you — 小王.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ de gōngyù tài xiǎo le.
Wǒ yǒu yí ge xīn shǒujī.

notes.text: Only for objects. For people, 老 (lǎo).

examples.pinyin: Wǒ de diànnǎo tài jiù le.

notes.text: Also a familiar prefix — 老王, 老板, 老公.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ yéye yǐjīng hěn lǎo le.
examples.english: My grandpa is already very old.

notes.text: Also "honored" in polite phrases — 您贵姓? = what is your (esteemed) surname?

examples.pinyin: Zhèlǐ de kāfēi tài guì le.
examples.english: The coffee here is too expensive.

notes.text: Note the reading: 便 is pián here, not biàn as in 方便.

examples.hanzi: 这个市场的水果很便宜。
examples.pinyin: Zhège shìchǎng de shuǐguǒ hěn piányi.
examples.english: The fruit at this market is cheap.

notes.text: The all-purpose positive. Stacks onto verbs to form adjectives: 好吃, 好喝, 好看, 好玩.
好 + 吃 (to eat). For drinks it is 好喝 (hǎohē) — Chinese keeps them separate.

examples.hanzi: 这家餐厅的烤鸭很好吃。
examples.pinyin: Zhè jiā cāntīng de kǎoyā hěn hǎochī.
examples.english: The roast duck at this restaurant is delicious.

notes.text: Works for people, clothes, movies — anything worth looking at.
For places and activities.

examples.english: This game is a lot of fun.

notes.text: 高兴 (gāoxìng) is close; 开心 is the more everyday "in good spirits."
难 (difficult) + 过 (to pass) — literally "hard to get through."

examples.english: He broke up and he's really sad.

notes.text: 美 (měi) is more formal/aesthetic.
可 (-able) + 爱 (to love) — "loveable."
Also used for anything cool or slickly done.

examples.pinyin: Tā de nán péngyou hěn shuài.

notes.text: Same character as in 难过 and 难看 (ugly).
Also "soon" — 快到了 = almost there. Do not confuse it with its homophone 块 (kuài), the spoken unit of money.
慢慢来 = take your time, one of the most-used phrases in the language.
Note the reading: cháng = long, zhǎng = to grow (长大).
For height, 矮 (ǎi).

examples.pinyin: Zhè tiáo kùzi tài duǎn le.

notes.text: For people and for heights/prices alike.
Also the verb "to quarrel" — 吵架 (chǎojià).
The same word as in 不太舒服 (feeling unwell) — comfort of body covers both.
方 (direction/way) + 便 (biàn here, not pián).
Also for personality/talk — 嘴甜 = sweet-talking.

examples.pinyin: Zhè bēi nǎichá tài tián le.
examples.english: This cup of milk tea is too sweet.
This soup is a bit salty.

notes.text: Also describes sore muscles — 腰酸.
Also "hardship" — 辛苦了 uses it.

examples.english: This cup of coffee is very bitter.

notes.text: Literally "has meaning." 没意思 = boring, the everyday counterpart to 无聊.

examples.pinyin: Zhè bù diànyǐng hěn yǒu yìsi.

notes.text: 重 (heavy) + 要 (to want/need).
免 (to exempt) + 费 (fee). Different from 有空 (free as in available).

examples.english: The subway is really crowded in the morning.

notes.text: A loan from English "cool." Same character as in 酷儿 (queer).

cards.english: to earn / to make a profit

examples.pinyin: tāmen mài nǎichá zhuàn le qián.

notes.text: Always, habitually. 一直 (yìzhí) is "continuously/all along" — 一直在等 = have been waiting the whole time.

Your "formal/informal" split is softer than it looks: 经常 and 常常 are near-interchangeable, with 经常 the more common in speech and 常常 leaning slightly literary. The genuinely informal one is 老是 (lǎoshì — fourth tone; lǎoshi would be 老实, "honest"), which carries a complaining tone: 他老是迟到.

examples.english: I often go to the gym.

notes.text: See 经常 above. 老是 (lǎoshì) is the casual, mildly exasperated version.
Sometimes. For "when I have time," 有空的时候 (yǒu kòng de shíhou) — 空 is free time, 时候 is the moment.

examples.pinyin: wǒ yǒu shíhou zài jiā gōngzuò.

notes.text: Less frequent than 有时候 — occasionally, now and then.

examples.english: I drink beer now and then.

notes.text: Literally "very few" — 我很少喝酒 = I rarely drink. 几乎不 (almost never) is the stronger form.
每 (every) + 隔 (to separate by): 每隔一天 = every other day, 每隔一周 = every other week.

examples.hanzi: 他每隔半个小时看一次手机。
examples.pinyin: tā měi gé bàn ge xiǎoshí kàn yí cì shǒujī.
examples.english: He checks his phone every half hour.

notes.text: For laying out points in order: 首先…其次…最后. In casual speech people just use 先 (xiān): 先吃饭, 然后…

examples.hanzi: 首先，我们去超市，然后回家。
examples.pinyin: shǒuxiān, wǒmen qù chāoshì, ránhòu huíjiā.
examples.english: First we'll go to the supermarket, then go home.

notes.text: The workhorse sequencer. 然后呢? = "and then?" keeps a story going.

examples.hanzi: 我们吃饭，然后去看电影。
examples.pinyin: wǒmen chīfàn, ránhòu qù kàn diànyǐng.
examples.english: We'll eat, and then go see a movie.

notes.text: 最 (most) + 后 (after). Also just means "last/final" — 最后一天.

examples.english: In the end, we went to a bar.

notes.text: The mirror of 以后 (yǐhòu). It follows the event: 吃饭(event)以前 = before eating. On its own it means "in the past."

examples.english: I brush my teeth before going to bed.

notes.text: one of the most common function words in Mandarin, meaning "then" in conditionals, or "right away/already" depending on context.
Carries relief after a wait — different from 最后, which is just sequential.
It follows the event: 吃饭(event)以后 = after eating.

examples.hanzi: 吃饭以后我们去散步吧。
examples.pinyin: Chīfàn yǐhòu wǒmen qù sànbù ba.
examples.english: Let's go for a walk after we eat.

notes.text: Wraps around a clause rather than introducing it: 我小的时候 = when I was little. The question word "when?" is 什么时候.

examples.hanzi: 我吃饭的时候不看手机。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ chīfàn de shíhou bú kàn shǒujī.
examples.english: I don't look at my phone when I'm eating.

examples.pinyin: Nà cì wǒmen qù le hǎitān.
examples.english: That time we went to the beach.

notes.text: 下次见 = see you next time.
一 shifts to yí before a fourth tone. Shortened to 上次 (shàng cì) in speech — the 一 usually drops. Same pattern for 这次, 下次.

examples.hanzi: 上一次我们去了动物园。
examples.pinyin: Shàng yí cì wǒmen qù le dòngwùyuán.
examples.english: Last time we went to the zoo.

notes.text: 几 covers small counts. 好几次 (hǎo jǐ cì) = quite a few times.

examples.hanzi: 我去过那个博物馆几次。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ qù guo nàge bówùguǎn jǐ cì.
examples.english: I've been to that museum a few times.

notes.text: Nearly always pairs with a sentence-final 了: 我已经吃了.
后天 (hòutiān) = the day after tomorrow.

examples.english: I have to go to work tomorrow.

notes.text: 前天 (qiántiān) = the day before yesterday. Note how 前/后 map onto time the same way they map onto space.
以前 = before/previously (also row above); 过去 = the past as a stretch of time, and literally "to go over."

examples.english: I used to live in the countryside.

notes.text: Describes how something was before a change - 我原本想去 (I originally wanted to go). Often sets up a contrast with what actually happened.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ yuánběn xiǎng qù, kěshì xiàyǔ le.

examples.pinyin: Xiǎo de shíhou wǒ chángcháng qù gōngyuán.
examples.english: When I was little, I often went to the park.

notes.text: 刚 (gāng) alone before a verb also means "just did": 我刚到.

examples.pinyin: Tā gāngcái gěi wǒ dǎ diànhuà le.

examples.hanzi: 因为下雨，所以我不去了。
examples.pinyin: Yīnwèi xiàyǔ, suǒyǐ wǒ bú qù le.
examples.english: Because it's raining, I'm not going anymore.

examples.pinyin: Zhège hěn guì, dànshì hěn hǎochī.
examples.english: This is expensive, but it's delicious.

examples.hanzi: 我很累，可是我还要工作。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ hěn lèi, kěshì wǒ hái yào gōngzuò.
examples.english: I'm tired, but I still have to work.

examples.hanzi: 如果明天下雨，我就不去了。
examples.pinyin: Rúguǒ míngtiān xiàyǔ, wǒ jiù bú qù le.
examples.english: If it rains tomorrow, I won't go.

examples.hanzi: 只要你有空，我们就去看电影。
examples.pinyin: Zhǐyào nǐ yǒu kòng, wǒmen jiù qù kàn diànyǐng.
examples.english: As long as you're free, we'll go see a movie.

examples.hanzi: 今天下雨，所以我不去公园了。
examples.pinyin: Jīntiān xiàyǔ, suǒyǐ wǒ bú qù gōngyuán le.
examples.english: It's raining today, so I'm not going to the park.

notes.text: Two common uses: still (我还是不明白 = I still dont understand); or in either-or questions (你要茶还是咖啡 = tea or coffee?). Traditional form is 還是.

examples.english: Do you want tea or coffee?

notes.text: 跟我一起去 = come with me. 和 (hé) also works; 跟 is more spoken, especially in the north.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ gēn péngyou qù gōngyuán le.
examples.english: I went to the park with a friend.

notes.text: Joins nouns only — never two sentences. For linking clauses use 然后 (then) or 而且 (moreover).

examples.pinyin: Wǒ yǒu yì zhī māo hé yì zhī gǒu.
examples.english: I have a cat and a dog.

notes.text: The default reaction of mild surprise or interest — said constantly in conversation, much lighter than English "really?" can sound.

examples.pinyin: Zhēn de ma? Nǐ yào jiéhūn le?

notes.text: 几次 expects a small number, 多少次 is open-ended. Note it overlaps with "a few times" — 几 both asks and answers.

examples.hanzi: 你去过那个博物馆几次？
examples.pinyin: Nǐ qù guo nàge bówùguǎn jǐ cì?
examples.english: How many times have you been to that museum?

notes.text: 多 (how) + 久 (long in time). 多长时间 (duō cháng shíjiān) means the same thing, a touch more explicit.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ zài zhèlǐ zhù le duō jiǔ?
examples.english: How long have you lived here?

examples.hanzi: 怎么说呢，这个电影有点儿奇怪。
examples.pinyin: Zěnme shuō ne, zhège diànyǐng yǒudiǎnr qíguài.
examples.english: How should I put it... this movie is a bit strange.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ chángcháng yùndòng, bǐrú pǎobù hé yóuyǒng.
examples.english: I often exercise, for example running and swimming.

examples.pinyin: Duì wǒ lái shuō, kāichē hěn nán.

notes.text: The everyday way to introduce an opinion or feeling — softer and more common in speech than 我认为.

examples.hanzi: 我觉得这个火锅很好吃。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ juéde zhège huǒguō hěn hǎochī.
examples.english: I think this hotpot is delicious.

examples.english: So here's the thing: I have to work overtime tomorrow.

notes.text: A hedge — "not necessarily / we'll see." Common as a standalone reply.

examples.pinyin: Tā míngtiān huì qù ma? Yīnggāi ba.

notes.text: Softens a statement into an impression rather than a fact — sits before the thing it hedges: 好像下雨了 (seems like it's raining).

examples.english: It seems like it's raining outside.

notes.text: Verb "to give," and also the preposition "to/for" before the recipient: 给我打电话 = call me.

examples.pinyin: Māma gěi wǒ yì běn shū.

notes.text: Goes after an adjective or verb: 贵一点儿 = a bit more expensive. Contrast 有点儿, which goes before and leans negative: 有点儿贵 = a bit too expensive.

examples.english: Can it be a little cheaper?

cards.hanzi: 我会 / 我要 / 我打算
cards.pinyin: wǒ huì / wǒ yào / wǒ dǎsuàn

notes.text: Three different futures: 会 = will (prediction or ability), 要 = going to (intention, firm), 打算 = plan to (deliberate). Mandarin has no tense, so the choice of these carries it.

examples.english: I'll go to the bank tomorrow.

notes.text: 想 = would like, soft and safe for requests. 要 = want, firmer and can sound demanding — fine when ordering food, blunt when asking a favor.

examples.english: I'd like to drink some coffee.

cards.english: wait a moment / in a bit

notes.text: 待会儿 (dāihuìr) is the northern spoken equivalent.

examples.pinyin: Děng yíxià wǒ gěi nǐ dǎ diànhuà.
examples.english: I'll call you in a bit.

notes.text: Pairs with 但是 in the second clause — Chinese keeps both halves: 虽然…但是… where English drops one.

examples.pinyin: Suīrán hěn guì, dànshì hěn hǎochī.

notes.text: Often paired with 不但 (not only): 不但…而且…

examples.hanzi: 这个餐厅很便宜,而且很好吃。
examples.pinyin: Zhège cāntīng hěn piányi, érqiě hěn hǎochī.
examples.english: This restaurant is cheap, and the food is good too.

notes.text: For statements. 还是 (háishì) is for questions — 茶还是咖啡? Getting these backwards is the classic mistake.

examples.hanzi: 我们可以喝茶或者咖啡。
examples.pinyin: Wǒmen kěyǐ hē chá huòzhě kāfēi.
examples.english: We can have tea or coffee.

notes.text: Softens a correction — 其实我不太喜欢.
Dismisses the preceding complication: 反正我都可以.
Also the noun "result." Often introduces an unexpected outcome.

examples.hanzi: 我没带雨伞,结果衣服都湿透了。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ méi dài yǔsǎn, jiéguǒ yīfu dōu shītòu le.
examples.english: I didn't bring an umbrella, and as a result my clothes got soaked.

notes.text: Restates or clarifies what you just said.

examples.hanzi: 他明天休假,也就是说他不上班。
examples.pinyin: Tā míngtiān xiūjià, yě jiù shì shuō tā bú shàngbān.
examples.english: He's off tomorrow, which means he isn't going to work.

notes.text: Said when something pops into your head mid-conversation. Literally "correct" — the pivot is idiomatic.

examples.pinyin: Duìle, nǐ míngtiān yǒu kòng ma?
examples.english: By the way, are you free tomorrow?

notes.text: 特别 alone = especially/particularly.

examples.hanzi: 我经常运动,特别是跑步。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ jīngcháng yùndòng, tèbié shì pǎobù.

notes.text: 要是 is the spoken counterpart to 如果; 就 picks up the consequence.

examples.hanzi: 要是明天下雨,我们就不去了。
examples.pinyin: Yàoshi míngtiān xiàyǔ, wǒmen jiù bú qù le.
examples.english: If it rains tomorrow, we won't go.

notes.text: 一到就走 = left as soon as he arrived. Two very common function words doing a lot of work.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ yí dào jiā jiù shuìjiào le.
examples.english: I went to sleep as soon as I got home.

notes.text: 同 (same) + 时 (time).

examples.english: We arrived at the airport at the same time.

notes.text: More formal than 因为; common in writing.

examples.hanzi: 由于下雨,我们没去公园。
examples.pinyin: Yóuyú xiàyǔ, wǒmen méi qù gōngyuán.
examples.english: Because of the rain, we didn't go to the park.

notes.text: Goes at the front: 为了省钱, 我自己做饭.

examples.english: To stay fit, I often go running.

notes.text: Very close to 原本 above — 本来 is the more common in speech.

examples.hanzi: 我本来想去，可是我太累了。
examples.pinyin: wǒ běnlái xiǎng qù, kěshì wǒ tài lèi le.
examples.english: I was originally going to go, but I was too tired.

notes.text: Also "possible/possibility." 大概 (dàgài) and 应该 (yīnggāi) cover similar hedging ground.
Said on realizing why something was the case.

examples.hanzi: 怪不得你很累，你昨天加班了。
examples.pinyin: guàibude nǐ hěn lèi, nǐ zuótiān jiābān le.
examples.english: No wonder you're tired, you worked overtime yesterday.

examples.pinyin: wǒ hěn qīdài zhè cì lǚyóu.
examples.english: I'm really looking forward to this trip.
You really must get some rest.

notes.text: 都可以 answers "which one/where/when" questions by saying every option is fine — interchangeable with 随便你 but slightly more neutral, less deferential.

examples.english: I'm fine with anything to drink.

notes.text: 有空 = to have free time. The standard opener for proposing to meet up.

examples.hanzi: 你有空吗？咱们去逛街吧。
examples.pinyin: nǐ yǒu kòng ma? zánmen qù guàngjiē ba.
examples.english: Are you free? Let's go shopping.

notes.text: 生日快乐 = happy birthday.
早餐 (zǎocān) is the slightly more formal/menu word.
国产剧 (guóchǎnjù, "domestically produced drama") is what people actually say. Genres: 古装剧 (period/costume), 都市剧 (urban/contemporary). By the same pattern 韩剧 = K-drama, 美剧 = US shows, 日剧 = J-drama.

examples.hanzi: 我在看一部中国电视剧。
examples.pinyin: wǒ zài kàn yí bù Zhōngguó diànshìjù.

notes.text: Basic word for a class/lesson.

examples.pinyin: wǒ wǎnshang hěn shǎo chūqù wán.
examples.english: I rarely go out in the evening.

notes.text: Also means "embarrassed": 我不好意思说 = I'm too embarrassed to say.
过节 (guòjié) = to celebrate a holiday. 春节 = Spring Festival/Lunar New Year.

examples.hanzi: 今天是节日，商场很热闹。
examples.pinyin: Jīntiān shì jiérì, shāngchǎng hěn rènao.
examples.english: Today is a holiday, so the mall is really lively.

notes.text: The universal shopping question.

examples.english: How much is this cup of milk tea?

notes.text: The potential complement — 不 slots between verb and result to mean "cannot." 看不见 = unable to see vs 没看见 = didn't see. The positive form is 看得见 (can see).

examples.pinyin: Nǐ zài nǎr? Wǒ kàn bu jiàn nǐ.
examples.english: Where are you? I can't see you.

notes.text: 见 as a result complement = perceived. 听见 (heard it) vs 听懂 (understood it) — you can do the first without the second, which is exactly the learner's situation.
Same pattern as 听见. 没 negates completed actions, never 不.

examples.pinyin: Yàoshi zài nǎr? Wǒ méi kànjiàn.
examples.english: Where are the keys? I didn't see them.

notes.text: 懂 is a result complement: 听懂 = understood by listening, 看懂 = understood by reading. 我不明白 (wǒ bù míngbai) is different — it means the idea itself does not make sense to you, not that you missed the words.
不知道 on its own is fine as a full reply.

examples.pinyin: Tā zài nǎr? Wǒ bù zhīdào.
examples.english: Where is he? I don't know.

notes.text: 听 (hear) + 说 (say) — "I heard it said that…". Introduces secondhand information: 我听说他要搬家.

examples.hanzi: 我听说那家餐厅很好吃。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ tīngshuō nà jiā cāntīng hěn hǎochī.
examples.english: I heard that restaurant is really good.

cards.english: I'll get it / let me handle it

notes.text: 我来 = I'll do it (the action is implied by context — paying the bill, carrying something, answering the door).

examples.pinyin: Wǒ lái ba, nǐ xiūxi ba.
examples.english: I've got it — you take a rest.

notes.text: The standard reply to an apology or minor mishap — literally "no connection/relevance" (i.e., it doesn't matter).

examples.hanzi: 对不起，我迟到了。没关系。
examples.pinyin: Duìbuqǐ, wǒ chídào le. Méi guānxi.

notes.text: 说好了 = we've agreed on this already. Used to confirm a plan is locked in, sometimes with a light "no backing out" undertone.

examples.pinyin: Shuō hǎo le, míngtiān wǒ qǐngkè.
examples.english: It's settled — tomorrow it's my treat.

notes.text: Doubling the verb (想想) softens it into "have a little think" — a very common move in Mandarin.

examples.hanzi: 我们去哪儿吃饭？让我想想。
examples.pinyin: Wǒmen qù nǎr chīfàn? Ràng wǒ xiǎngxiang.
examples.english: Where should we go to eat? Let me think.

notes.text: 改天 = some other day. A polite way to postpone plans without giving a firm reason.

examples.hanzi: 我今天很忙，我们改天吧。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ jīntiān hěn máng, wǒmen gǎitiān ba.
examples.english: I'm really busy today, let's do another day.

notes.text: 中学 (middle/secondary school) + 生 (student). 小学生 = primary schooler, 大学生 = university student.

examples.english: My younger sister is a middle school student.

notes.text: 上午 (shàngwǔ) covers late morning up to noon.

examples.english: I get up at seven in the morning.

notes.text: Interchangeable with 没关系 in most situations; a touch more casual.

examples.hanzi: 这个太贵了，有其他的吗？
examples.pinyin: Zhège tài guì le, yǒu qítā de ma?
examples.english: This one is too expensive — do you have any others?

notes.text: The natural everyday way to say other people/someone else - used constantly in casual speech. Contrast with 其他人 (qítārén), which leans toward the rest of the people in a specific group rather than people in general.
号码 = number (as an identifier). 手机号 (shǒujīhào) is the everyday short form.

examples.pinyin: nǐ de diànhuà hàomǎ shì duōshao?

notes.text: 改 (to change) + 天 (day) — "some other day." The polite soft-postpone, as in 我们改天吧.

examples.hanzi: 我今天很忙，我们改天去吧。
examples.pinyin: wǒ jīntiān hěn máng, wǒmen gǎitiān qù ba.
examples.english: I'm busy today, let's go some other day.

notes.text: For real apologies. 不好意思 (bù hǎoyìsi) is the lighter "excuse me / my bad," used far more often.
暴 (violent/sudden) + 雨 (rain). 台风 (táifēng) = typhoon, 雷阵雨 (léizhènyǔ) = thunderstorm.

examples.pinyin: zuótiān xià le yì chǎng bàoyǔ.

notes.text: 谢谢你 adds the person. 不客气 (bú kèqi) = you're welcome.
夸张 = exaggerated. Used for reacting to something excessive, whether outrageous news or someone being dramatic.

examples.hanzi: 一杯咖啡一百块？太夸张了！
examples.pinyin: yì bēi kāfēi yìbǎi kuài? tài kuāzhāng le!
examples.english: A hundred kuai for one coffee? That's ridiculous!

notes.text: For replying to a message, 回复 (huífù) or just 回.

examples.english: You need to apologize to her.

notes.text: 问问题 = to ask a question. 请问 = "may I ask," the standard opener to a stranger.
Three "cans": 可以 (permitted), 会 (learned skill), 能 (physically able).
空 is kòng (free time) here, not kōng (empty). 没空 = busy/not available.
迟 (late) + 到 (to arrive).

examples.english: He was late for work again.

notes.text: 带伞 = bring an umbrella. Also "to lead" — 带你去.

examples.pinyin: xiàyǔ le, nǐ dài yǔsǎn ba.

notes.text: 换钱 = to exchange money, 换衣服 = to change clothes.
Split from your combined "打扫 / 收拾" entry. Usually implies sweeping/cleaning a space (floors, surfaces).

examples.english: I need to clean the kitchen today.

notes.text: Same 洗 as 洗脸, 洗澡, 洗手.

examples.pinyin: wǒ zài zhǎo wǒ de yàoshi.

notes.text: 我忘了 = I forgot.

examples.pinyin: wǒ wàng le tā de diànhuà hàomǎ.

examples.english: I get up at seven in the morning.

notes.text: 送 covers giving as a gift and seeing someone off — 送你回家 = to walk you home. For simply handing something over, 给 (gěi).
去 (to go there) vs 来 (lái, to come here) — Chinese picks the verb by where the speaker is standing. 去年 = last year.

examples.english: Let's go to the park tomorrow.

notes.text: 回 (to return). 回来 = to come back, 回去 = to go back.

examples.english: I go home after I get off work.

notes.text: 帮我一下 = give me a hand. 帮忙 (bāngmáng) is the verb-object form: 帮我一个忙.
赶时间 = to be pressed for time, 赶紧 (gǎnjǐn) = quickly, right away.

examples.english: We have to hurry to catch the train.

notes.text: Contrast 认识 (to know a person). 我不知道 = I don't know.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ zhīdào tā zài nǎr ma?
examples.english: Do you know where he is?

notes.text: Also the noun: 有什么安排? = what are your plans?

examples.english: What are your plans for the weekend?

examples.pinyin: Wǒ xūyào yí ge xīn shǒujī.

notes.text: 认识 = to know/be acquainted with a person or place. 知道 (zhīdào) = to know a fact. 我认识他 vs 我知道他 are different claims.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ rènshi tā de nǚ péngyou.

examples.hanzi: 你可以推荐一家餐厅吗？
examples.pinyin: Nǐ kěyǐ tuījiàn yì jiā cāntīng ma?

examples.hanzi: 我昨天在超市遇到了我的老师。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ zuótiān zài chāoshì yùdào le wǒ de lǎoshī.
examples.english: I ran into my teacher at the supermarket yesterday.

notes.text: 看 does a lot of work: 看书 (read), 看电影 (watch), 看病 (see a doctor), 看看 (take a look).

examples.pinyin: Nǐ kàn, nà shì wǒ de māo.

examples.hanzi: 我想报名参加这个活动。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng bàomíng cānjiā zhège huódòng.
examples.english: I want to sign up for this activity.

notes.text: 分 also means "minute" and "point/score," and 分手 (to break up) is literally "to part hands."

examples.pinyin: Zánmen fēn zhè pán jiǎozi ba.
examples.english: Let's split this plate of dumplings.

notes.text: 开 spans open/start/operate: 开门, 开会, 开车, 开始.

examples.english: What time does the supermarket open?
I take a shower after I run.

notes.text: Three senses: to think, to miss someone (我想你), and to want to (想去).

examples.english: I want to go to the park.

notes.text: 扔垃圾 = to take out the trash.

examples.english: I'll go take out the trash.

notes.text: leans toward organizing/putting things away rather than scrubbing. Note the tone difference from 首饰 (shǒushi, jewelry) above — easy to mix up.
试试看 = give it a try. 试衣服 = to try on clothes.

examples.pinyin: wǒ xiǎng shì zhè jiàn yīfu.
examples.english: I'd like to try on this piece of clothing.

notes.text: 明白了 = got it. 懂了 (dǒng le) works the same way.
不用 (búyòng) = no need — a very common polite refusal.

examples.pinyin: wǒ kěyǐ yòng nǐ de shǒujī ma?

examples.english: We're waiting in line to buy tickets.

notes.text: 随便 on its own means "whatever/however"; adding 你 makes it explicitly about deferring to the other person's choice.

examples.english: Where should we go? Up to you.

notes.text: 微 (micro) + 信 (message). 加微信 = to add someone on WeChat, the standard way to exchange contacts.

examples.pinyin: zhège zhōumò nǐ yǒu kòng ma?

notes.text: 那 here refers back to whatever was just mentioned; 还好 softens a judgment to "could be worse."

examples.pinyin: jiù yí ge xiǎoshí? nà hái hǎo.
examples.english: Only an hour? Well, that's not so bad.

notes.text: 几 asks for a small number, so it is the right question word for the hour. Answer with 点: 三点半 = 3:30, 三点一刻 = 3:15.

examples.english: Excuse me, what time is it?

notes.text: 说得对 uses 得 to attach the result (对, correct) to the verb 说 — literally "what you said comes out correct."

examples.pinyin: nǐ shuō de duì, zhège tài guì le.
examples.english: You're right, this is too expensive.

cards.english: You've worked hard / thanks for the effort

notes.text: Said to acknowledge someone's effort or hardship — after a long shift, a big task, or a hard trip. No single-word English equivalent.

examples.pinyin: nǐ jīntiān jiābān le, xīnkǔ le!
examples.english: You worked overtime today. Thanks for all your hard work!
